title: Down with Lag!
principle: Check audio latency separately from video
why: Sometimes only the sound is delayed; through a home theater system you might hear impact sounds a little late.
how: Use an analog audio connection or low-latency audio settings, and experiment if equipment doesn't get along.
quote: If you're using a home theater system, you might hear the impact sounds a little late.

title: Make the Tempo Match the Game
principle: Match music tempo to the speed of the game's action.
why: Some tempos fit a game's content and others don't; even among similar fighting games the right tempo varies with how fast the action is.
how: Measure each track's BPM; for fast battles aim around 130–170 BPM, as Smash Bros. battle arrangements do, and treat ~200 BPM as an exception.
example: Super Smash Bros. battle stage music, 130–170 BPM on average.
quote: Even among similar fighting games, the right tempo will vary depending on the speed of the action.

title: Make the Tempo Match the Game
principle: Vary tempo and rhythm between scenes within the same game.
why: Different scenes in one game call for different tempos and rhythms, and tempo can reinforce what the player is going through.
how: Assign a target tempo per scene; for example, slow the music as the player goes deeper into a dungeon, as the first Dragon Quest did.
example: Dragon Quest, where dungeon music slows the deeper you go.
quote: Of course, the same applies within one single game, where different scenes will call for certain tempos and rhythms.

title: Fun Beyond Game Essence
principle: Use a few simple sounds to imply a world beyond the screen.
why: As a game approaches real life, players perceive more information than is actually shown, which deepens the experience.
how: Trigger a handful of simple, well-timed sound effects, like doors clattering and feet shuffling, to suggest offscreen activity.
example: A train simulator arriving at a station.
quote: All the program does is call a handful of simple sound effects, but it really feels like the doors are opening and people are getting on board

title: Strike a Balance with Sound Effects
principle: Make sounds louder the more relevant they are to the player.
why: Match-deciding events and direct feedback for the player's actions matter most; judging only by the size of an action can give the wrong result.
how: Rank effects (KO > hits > specials and voices > dodges and blocks > swings > landing > jump > walk) and mix in that order.
anti_pattern: Setting volume by the action's physical size alone.
example: Super Smash Bros.' sound priority order.
quote: The more relevant a sound is to the player, the louder that sound should be.

title: Strike a Balance with Sound Effects
principle: Make landing sounds louder than jump sounds.
why: Landing is a reaction, so it gets more emphasis than the jump that caused it.
how: Mix landings above jumps, and give each character landing sounds that match their clothing or footwear.
example: Cloud's landing sounds, which differ by costume.
quote: Since landing is a reaction, we make it louder than the jump.

title: Strike a Balance with Sound Effects
principle: Make footsteps audible and varied by character and floor.
why: Barely audible footsteps make characters feel like they're hovering, one repeated effect sounds mechanical, and believable sounds feel best.
how: Record several footstep variants per character and per floor material, and rotate between them.
anti_pattern: Silent or single-sample footsteps.
example: Unique footsteps for every Smash fighter.
quote: You can barely hear them in a lot of games, making it feel like something is missing— as if your character is hovering, not walking.

title: Listen in Various Environments
principle: Check sound on headphones, PC speakers and a cheap TV
why: TV speakers are the most common setup and lose low frequencies; details tuned only in a pristine studio may be inaudible on everyday speakers.
how: Compare every important sound across several listening environments and fix the problems found in each before approving it.
anti_pattern: Finalizing sound solely on big studio speakers.
quote: More than anything, I recommend not solely using big studio speakers to finalize sound.

title: Listen in Various Environments
principle: Keep a fixed listening reference throughout the project
why: If your listening standard changes, it becomes hard to stay consistent with all the audio you checked before.
how: Use the same reference headphones and speakers from start to finish; delay upgrading them until the project is done.
anti_pattern: Switching reference headphones partway through a project.
quote: If your standard changes, it'll be tough to align with all the audio that you checked previously.

title: Listen in Various Environments
principle: Balance multi-environment fixes against your creative vision
why: Taking the tuning too far can pull you away from the sound you intended, and some outputs matter less (the Switch speakers are already crisp, and many handheld players play muted).
how: Prioritize the environments most players use, and aim for a balance that works across them rather than optimizing for any single speaker.
anti_pattern: Over-tuning for one weak speaker until the creative vision is lost.
example: Nintendo Switch built-in speakers
quote: If you take this sound tuning too far, you might stray from your creative vision, so focus on finding a good balance that works in multiple environments.

title: Listen in Various Environments
principle: When borrowing a sound, match how it sounded on original hardware
why: Mimicking the original game's audio wasn't enough for Ryu; the team wanted to capture how it sounded coming from the arcade cabinet.
how: Reference the source as players heard it on its original hardware, and expect careful trial and error.
example: Ryu's impact sounds in Smash Bros.
quote: we also wanted to capture how it sounded coming from the arcade cabinet— a process that required lots of careful trial and error.

title: Game Music and Ambient Sounds
principle: Build the soundtrack on a main theme and its arrangements
why: Huge soundtracks are harder to remember or get excited by, and a song has more impact when people can remember its melody.
how: Write one main theme, then reuse arrangements of it across the game instead of producing many unrelated songs.
anti_pattern: Producing too many songs for a single game.
quote: However you do it, a song will have more impact if people can remember its melody.

title: Game Music and Ambient Sounds
principle: Back realistic visuals with realistic ambient sound, each layer given proper presence
why: As graphics carried more visual information, music that stood out too much started to feel off; realistic graphics call for realistic ambience.
how: Layer sounds like wind through leaves, feet on dirt and clinking armor, and mix each element to an appropriate level under the music.
anti_pattern: Loud, foreground music fighting with detailed visuals.
example: NES-style music played over modern games sounds noisy and off.
quote: Realistic graphics, for example, call for realistic ambient sounds.

title: Game Music and Ambient Sounds
principle: Make each song complement how the player is feeling
why: The right approach depends on the game type, but music works best when it supports the player's emotional state.
how: For each scene, note what the player should feel there and check that its music reinforces that feeling.
quote: In any case, I'd say it's best to make songs that complement how the player is feeling.

title: Audio as Fiction and Non-Fiction
principle: Exaggerate impact sounds instead of using realistic ones
why: Real punches would sound like a bunch of slaps, and forgetting that fighting games aren't real fighting pulls you away from the essence you want.
how: Design combat hits as exaggerated sounds and compare them against realistic recordings to confirm they carry more weight.
anti_pattern: Literal realism in combat audio.
example: Street Fighter II's impact sounds are incredibly fake but effective.
quote: If you don't remember right from the start that fighting games are nothing like actual fighting, you'll end up drifting far away from the game essence you want.

title: Audio as Fiction and Non-Fiction
principle: Use realistic material sounds to fill in what simple graphics can't show
why: Lifelike sounds help players fill in missing information, giving meaning and weight to otherwise simple visuals.
how: Give each material and action its own realistic sound, such as different sounds for placing wood and stone.
example: Minecraft's building sounds let you feel the weight of wood and stone despite cube graphics.
quote: The relatively lifelike sound effects help people to fill in the gaps in information.

title: Audio as Fiction and Non-Fiction
principle: Balance sound exaggeration against how realistic the visuals are
why: The more realistic the visuals, the stranger exaggerated sounds feel, and the right balance makes the world feel more substantial.
how: Decide per sound category whether its job is impact or information, and tune exaggeration to the game's visual realism.
quote: Sound effects can be either exaggerated or realistic. By finding the right balance in your game, you can really help make its world feel more substantial.

title: Praise the Player!
principle: Add subtle crowd reactions to near-misses and close saves
why: Smash's crowd gives a subtle "oh!" when you barely manage to grab a ledge, acknowledging the close call in the moment.
how: Trigger quiet gasps on narrow escapes and louder cheers on big launches and KOs.
example: Super Smash Bros.: the crowd's "oh!" on a barely-made ledge grab.

title: Voice Recording
principle: Script every vocalization, down to each grunt
why: Sessions are short (about an hour per Smash fighter), and anything not in the script won't get recorded.
how: List basics (attacks, jumps, damage reactions) and unique lines (special moves, Final Smashes, reveal dialogue), plus reference audio from the original game.
anti_pattern: Leaving small grunts and reactions out of the script.
example: Super Smash Bros. voice scripts.
quote: Every “ha" or “hmph” needs to be on there in order to get recorded.

title: Voice Recording
principle: Keep in-battle voice lines short and sparse
why: Longer lines or excessive chatter in battle draw too much attention and break player immersion.
how: Cap combat lines to short barks and limit how often they trigger.
anti_pattern: Long lines and constant chatter during gameplay.
example: Super Smash Bros. fighter voices.
quote: Longer lines or excessive chatter in battle can draw too much attention and break player immersion.

title: Voice Recording
principle: Plan how voices overlap so they don't compete
why: It's not good to have voices competing with each other, especially loud, feral-sounding ones.
how: Test simultaneous vocalizations from multiple characters and adjust timing or volume where they clash.
anti_pattern: Voices stacking and fighting for attention.
example: Super Smash Bros.: Bowser and Donkey Kong.

title: Voice Recording
principle: Budget heavy editing time after recording
why: Surprisingly, it's after recording that things really get busy, as voices are edited over and over to suit the game.
how: Schedule post-session editing as a major task, not an afterthought.
quote: Surprisingly, it's after the recording that things really get busy, as voices get edited over and over to make them suitable for the game.

title: ♪ PRESS START
principle: Keep the performance central; use game footage only occasionally
why: At PRESS START, playing video after video would have distracted from the point of the concert, the performance itself.
how: In any music showcase, treat footage as an occasional accent and let the live music carry the event.
anti_pattern: Running game video behind every piece.
example: PRESS START game music concerts (2006-2016).

title: ♪ PRESS START
principle: Curate from a large candidate pool, then narrow down together
why: As the committee member most familiar with games, Sakurai brought plenty of samples to meetings so the group could listen and narrow them down before arranging.
how: Gather many more candidate tracks than you have slots, review them as a group, and only then commission arrangements.
example: PRESS START song selection meetings.

title: Arranging Music
principle: Keep the original main melody intact in every arrangement
why: Players come to hear this one song out of many; arrangements that change the piece totally disappoint, like the Star Wars theme changing with each film.
how: Require that humming the arrangement is like humming the original, and flag mistranscriptions in review.
anti_pattern: Changing a melody because the original feels antiquated.
example: Disappointing game-music arrangement CDs; the Star Wars theme analogy.
quote: Even if the original feels antiquated to you, and even if you have the urge to change it, make sure you maintain the piece's identity.

title: Arranging Music
principle: Brief arrangers with structural rules drawn from gameplay
why: Smash needs competitive tempo and energy, an intro for the "3, 2, 1, GO!" countdown, big shifts for a dynamic game, a climax, and a length fitting two-minute (2.5 in Ultimate) timed matches.
how: Give composers a written brief: tempo, intro or post-countdown start, dynamic shifts, end-climax, loop point and target length matching a typical match.
example: Super Smash Bros. arrangement guidelines.

title: The Original Piece is Always Right
principle: Treat the original as heard in-game as the authority when arranging
why: Players' memories come from playing the original, so an arrangement must not detract from their past experience, however unconventional the original is.
how: Identify the main melody and key features by what players heard in the game (and its ports), and reproduce quirks like an on-beat/off-beat shift faithfully.
anti_pattern: Letting music theory overrule what the original actually sounded like.
example: Athena: Sakurai heard melody A as the main melody, while musically it was B. Its on-beat/off-beat shift was reproduced in Smash.
quote: However you cut it, when arranging beloved songs, the original piece is always right.

title: The Original Piece is Always Right
principle: Mirror the original's hardware-driven structure in arrangements
why: In the original Psycho Soldier, the music switched to the internal audio processor after the first verse, and that shape is part of what players remember.
how: Where the original lost vocals or changed character because of the hardware, use an instrumental section there, and keep separate language versions with their own verse counts and intonation.
anti_pattern: Normalizing a song's structure to modern conventions.
example: Psycho Soldier in Smash Ultimate: Japanese recreates three verses. English plays verse one, an instrumental, then verse one again.

title: Strong Attack, Light Reverb
principle: Make impact sounds reach a strong level almost immediately
why: An impact sound must never feel late, because players need a reaction to their attack right away; it can't literally start at peak volume, but must get to a strong sound almost immediately.
how: Shorten the attack of hit sounds so they peak at the very beginning.
anti_pattern: Hit sounds that swell in slowly and feel late.
example: Super Smash Bros. — impact sound revisions
quote: It's vital that players get a reaction to their attack right away.

title: Strong Attack, Light Reverb
principle: Keep reverb tails short so overlapping hits stay distinct
why: With four to eight players, sounds overlap constantly; long echoes feel strong but get lost and bury the next sound in noise, so rapid jabs are trimmed to just feel like consecutive hits.
how: Trim reverb on impact sounds in busy scenes and cut multi-hit sounds to the shortest length that still reads as separate hits.
anti_pattern: Long, echoing tails that sound great alone but muddy the mix.
example: Super Smash Bros. — rapid jab sounds pared down
quote: Next, don't drag out the reverberation too much.

title: Strong Attack, Light Reverb
principle: Finish a heavy hit's sound during hitstop, before action resumes
why: Strong attacks freeze the screen for hitstop while the sound keeps playing; ideally the main part of the sound is over before the action resumes.
how: Time heavy-hit sounds so their main body plays out within the hitstop freeze.
example: Super Smash Bros. — strong attacks with hitstop
quote: The sound keeps playing in the meantime, but ideally the main part of the sound effect should be over before the action resumes.

title: Strong Attack, Light Reverb
principle: Choose sounds that serve your game, not just sounds that are good
why: 'Strong attack, light reverb' fits Smash's crowded, fast battles; the right choice depends on the game, so the goal is the type of sound that best serves it.
how: Judge sound effects in the game's real worst-case context rather than in isolation.
anti_pattern: Picking sounds because they sound good on their own.
quote: it's not just about creating "good" sounds— it's also about finding the right type of sounds to best serve your game.

title: Giving Feedback for Sound Effects
principle: Request sounds with concrete roles, known comparisons and example links
why: Audio has no physical form and can't be approximated by voice, and not everyone knows every specific real sound.
how: Describe the role ('strong attack'), compare only to universally known sounds ('like a jet engine'), and attach a link such as a YouTube clip of a similar sound.
anti_pattern: Assuming the team knows the specific sound you mean.

title: Giving Feedback for Sound Effects
principle: Don't rely on onomatopoeia alone in written sound feedback
why: With remote work, asking for more 'clang' or 'boom' shows you had something in mind but doesn't convey it; still, onomatopoeia can sometimes bridge sound and emotion.
how: Use onomatopoeia only as an extra clue next to a concrete description, since the team wants as many details as possible.
anti_pattern: Emails that just ask for more clang or boom.
example: Sakurai's sound lead said onomatopoeia can be helpful every now and then.
quote: There's little point in writing an email asking for more clang or boom.

title: Giving Feedback for Sound Effects
principle: Approve sounds that fit the game even if they differ from your idea
why: Sounds directly convey feedback and feeling, so fit matters most, and sometimes the result is better than what was imagined.
how: Judge each delivered sound by whether it suits the game, while starting every request with a clear idea of the target.
anti_pattern: Rejecting sounds only because they don't match the one in your head.

title: Balancing Ambient Sounds
principle: Mix ambient sounds lowest so key sound effects stay audible
why: Ambient sounds are the least important, so if they stand out, players can't hear the sound effects that really matter.
how: Give ambience the lowest priority and volume in your mix, and verify that no gameplay-critical effect is ever masked.
anti_pattern: Ambience loud or busy enough to bury important effects.
example: Smash Bros. stages contain many ambient sounds that are hard to hear at normal volume.
quote: Hence, if they stand out too much, you won't be able to hear the sound effects that really matter— and that's a problem.

title: Balancing Ambient Sounds
principle: Never leave dead silence; layer subtle ambience for immersion
why: Silence when the player stops kills the atmosphere, players with good speakers will notice the ambience, and immersion matters most in first-person or over-the-shoulder views.
how: Stop in each area and listen, and add quiet environmental layers wherever you hear nothing, especially in first-person or over-the-shoulder games.
anti_pattern: Dead silence whenever the action pauses.
quote: Additionally, if you stop playing for a second and hear nothing but dead silence, there'll be no sense of atmosphere.

title: Balancing Ambient Sounds
principle: Use realistic recordings for ambience, exaggerated sounds for actions
why: Unlike other sound effects, which generally need exaggeration, fairly realistic audio works well for ambience, even in cartoony games.
how: Use realistic environmental recordings for ambience and layer them under your stylized gameplay effects.
quote: As opposed to other sound effects which generally need to be more exaggerated, relatively realistic audio works great for ambient sounds.

title: Using Other Songs for Audio Reference
principle: Give composers a reference track and name what to keep from it
why: A concrete example helps a composer know where to start, but composers often can't tell which parts of a reference to keep or change, which is a common way to lose sight of the goal.
how: Name the quality you want (e.g., the surfer feel of The Ventures) and the signature parts not to copy (e.g., the famous guitar riff).
anti_pattern: Handing over a song with only "make it like this".
example: God Hand's "Gene's Rock-a-Bye" was asked for in the style of The Ventures; the iconic riff was left out but the surfer sound stayed.

title: Using Other Songs for Audio Reference
principle: Don't let one reference track close off other musical possibilities
why: A director fixated on a single piece closes their mind to alternatives, and everything ends up sounding like a cheap imitation.
how: Treat the reference as a starting point and judge drafts by how well they serve the game, staying flexible about the result.
anti_pattern: Rejecting every draft that doesn't sound like the reference.
quote: Everything will sound like a cheap imitation— and you can't lock yourself down like that.

title: Using Other Songs for Audio Reference
principle: License an existing song when it matches the game's theme exactly
why: Sometimes an existing piece fits a game's theme so well that using it as-is beats any soundalike.
how: Negotiate with the rightsholders to use the original song.
example: Ore no Shikabane wo Koete Yuke uses "Hana", a song about flowers blooming and wilting, for a family cursed with a two-year lifespan; designer Mr. Masuda negotiated the rights.

title: Gameplay as Part of a Live Performance
principle: Plan music cues around gameplay segments of variable length
why: The Chapter 12 clear time depended on how fast the mid-boss died, so the orchestra had to align its performance with when Sakurai beat it.
how: Identify segments whose length varies and give the music cue points that wait for or follow the player's actual progress.
example: Kid Icarus: Uprising's Air Battles last five minutes, but the mid-boss made the exact timing vary.

title: Famicom and NES Audio
principle: Decide which music voice yields when sound effects need a channel
why: On the Famicom, music and sound effects shared the same five channels, so part of the music often cut out when an effect played.
how: When voices are limited, set a priority so the least important music part drops out for an effect.
example: Famicom games cut part of the music to play sound effects.

title: Famicom and NES Audio
principle: Match each sound role to the timbre that suits it
why: Crisp pulse waves carried most Famicom music, the mellow triangle wave suited bass lines, and noise suited hits, explosions, cheers and waves.
how: Assign tones by role: crisp tones for main parts, mellow tones for bass, noise for impacts and ambient effects.

title: No Masterpiece Has Bad Audio
principle: Treat audio as essential to quality, not optional polish
why: Masterpieces exist with bad graphics or even without coherent game essence, but Sakurai can't name a single one with bad audio design.
how: Give music and sound effects the same priority, schedule and attention as graphics.
anti_pattern: Taking audio lightly.
quote: And yet, I can't think of a single example of a masterpiece with bad audio design.

title: No Masterpiece Has Bad Audio
principle: Build audio that players will remember first
why: When people recall a game they loved, the music and sound effects are often the first things that come to mind; audio hits you right in the heart.
how: Benchmark your music and sound effects against what you remember from games you loved, and construct even simple effects with care.
example: Old games with only simple noise-based sound effects that still had well-constructed audio.
quote: Even more than the game itself, its visuals, or its characters— audio is what hits you right in the heart.
